title: Graph manipulation
blurb: Feature augmentation, virtual nodes/edges, neighbour & subgraph sampling

hook.title: Re-drawing the road map
hook.text: The map you were given is rarely the best map to *travel* on. No landmarks (features)? Label each town with a number. Roads too thin and winding (sparse)? Build a **highway hub** connected to every town, or add shortcuts over two-hop roads. A mega-city with a million roads (dense)? Don't query every road: **sample a few each time**. A whole continent (too large)? Work on a **small region** at a time.
hook.recall: Remember the road map: each problem has its fix: no features → augment features; too sparse → virtual edges/nodes; too dense → sample neighbours; too large → sample subgraphs.

explore.intro: Two tabs: a sparse chain with a virtual node, and a dense hub with neighbour sampling.
tasks: Make the path 30 nodes long. What is the end-to-end distance with and without a virtual node?
Sample 2 of the hub’s 8 neighbours several times.
explore.takeaway: Feature augmentation (constants or one-hot unique IDs); virtual edges (2-hop) and a virtual node (distance ≤ 2); neighbour sampling to cut cost; subgraph sampling when the graph doesn’t fit on a GPU.

build.prompt: Match each problem with its fix.
build.template: No node features → {0}.  Too sparse → {1}.  Too dense → {2}.  Too large → {3}.
build.explanation: Slide 25 lists exactly these four pairs.

questions.prompt: The input graph has only an adjacency matrix and no node features. Standard approaches:
options: Assign constant values, or unique IDs as one-hot vectors
questions.explanation: Label each town with a constant or a unique ID.

questions.prompt: Two nodes in a sparse graph have shortest-path distance 10. After adding a virtual node connected to **all** nodes, what is the distance between them?
questions.explanation: Via the hub: node → virtual node → node = 2 hops. The slide: all nodes then have a distance of 2.

questions.prompt: For a *too dense* graph with high-degree nodes the slides suggest:
options: Sample neighbours when doing message passing
questions.explanation: Randomly choose, e.g., 2 neighbours per step; cost drops greatly, embeddings stay similar.

options: Connecting 2-hop neighbours via virtual edges can turn an author–paper graph into an author–author collaboration graph
A virtual node connects to all nodes in the graph
Neighbour sampling greatly reduces computational cost
Adding a virtual node makes message passing in a sparse graph worse
questions.explanation: “Benefits: greatly improves message passing in sparse graphs.”

questions.prompt: For a graph too large to fit its computation graph on a GPU:
questions.explanation: Work on a small region at a time.

questions.prompt: *“Sampling a different set of neighbours each time makes the embeddings meaningless.”* What does the slide say?
options: Each time different nodes may be sampled, but we still get embeddings similar to using all the neighbours, with greatly reduced cost
questions.explanation: A random subset per step approximates the full neighbourhood.
